title: Find One First
child_idea: When we know what a group costs, we can find what one costs by sharing equally. Then we can find what any number of them cost.

topics: Multiplication and division word problems: divide within 20, multiply within 40 (Primary 1, Multiplication and Division, p. 31)
Count money in dollars (Primary 1, Money, p. 31): whole dollars only, no notes, coins or cents until Term 3
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. This is an added lesson (gap from the word-problem books analysis: the price or size of one from a group). Start here is Primary 1 content: share a total equally to find one (within 20), then multiply to find many (within 40), in whole dollars. BEYOND PRIMARY 1 ON PURPOSE: Think harder and Go further chain the two steps with different numbers (the price of 7 from the price of 3), use the words a dozen and such, ask how many can be bought, and compare the price of one in two shops. Owner decision, 22 Oct 2026: strong content with scaffolding, said plainly to families. Say this on the parent page and in the opening of the guide; do not describe the lesson as MOE-aligned or syllabus-aligned. Money is only whole dollars and $1 tokens (counters): no notes, coins or cents until Term 3. Vocabulary taught here: each, a dozen, such. This lesson also holds the 20-minute end-of-term check (minutes 37 to 57); the check key, the grown-up note and the record sheet are in the Check files. Contest tag (tutor only): price of one first, then many; how many can be bought; compare the price of one.

Think harder: find the price of 7 from the price of 3, use a dozen and such, and say how many can be bought.
Go further: one price from each of two groups, money left over, and which shop sells one for less.
Take the 20-minute end-of-term check on private paper.

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: share equally

blocks.text: Deal the counters one at a time. Same number on each plate.

slides.note: Twelve counters are shared equally onto 3 plates. Children deal counters one at a time (or imagine it). Ask: how many on each plate (4); 6 counters shared between 2 plates (3); 15 counters shared among 3 plates (5). Children answer aloud or with fingers. No writing, no marks. A child who is unsure deals real counters or small things onto three plates or three pieces of paper.

slides.title: Each and in all

blocks.text: Each bag has the same number.

slides.note: Three bags with 4 counters in each bag. We say each bag has 4, and in all means every bag together. Ask: how many counters in all (12); 5 bags with 2 in each bag (10); 4 groups of 5 (20). This is Lessons 15 and 18 taught again. A child who is unsure adds one bag at a time and says the total each time.

slides.title: A strip of equal parts

blocks.text: 4 equal parts. The whole strip is 20.

slides.note: A strip is cut into 4 equal parts, and the whole strip is 20. Ask: how big is each part (5); 3 parts of 5 (15); 6 shared into 2 equal parts (3). This is Lesson 18 taught again: a strip shows equal groups. A child who is unsure counts 5, 10, 15, 20 on fingers and counts the fingers.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: 4 pencils cost $8.
How much does 1 pencil cost?
You may use counters.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: 3 apples cost $6.
How much do 5 apples cost?

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (4 pencils for $8; 1 pencil is $2) is an access question: any child can share 8 counters onto 4 pencils. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson idea: find one first. 1 apple costs $2 and 5 apples cost $10. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera. There is no private chat. Answers: $2; $10. Do not reveal puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list.

slides.title: Explore: find one

items: 4 pens cost $20. Count out 20 tokens.
Share the tokens equally onto 4 pens.
How much does 1 pen cost?

slides.note: Round 1, about 4 minutes. Children use their $1 tokens (the kit page or counters) and 4 small things as the pens. 4 pens cost $20: they count out 20 tokens and deal them one at a time onto the 4 pens until every pen has the same. Ask: how much does 1 pen cost (5). Say: 1 pen costs $5, because $20 shared equally among 4 pens is $5 each. Money is whole dollars only, and a token stands for $1. If a family has no shop items, 4 pieces of paper are fine. Answer: $5.

slides.title: Find many

items: 1 pen costs $3. Put 3 tokens by each pen.
Do this for 4 pens.
Count all the tokens.

slides.note: Round 2, about 3.5 minutes. Now we know the cost of one: 1 pen costs $3. For 4 pens children put 3 tokens by each pen and count all the tokens (12). Ask: how much do 4 pens cost (12). Say: 4 groups of $3 is $12. Link to Lesson 15: groups of. Answer: $12. A child who loses count puts the tokens in a row of 3 and counts in 3s.

slides.title: Find one, then many

items: Find 1 pen first: share $20 into 4 equal parts.
Then take 3 parts.
How much do 3 pens cost?

slides.note: Round 3, about 3.5 minutes. 4 pens cost $20. How much do 3 pens cost? Children share 20 tokens onto 4 pens (5 each) and then take 3 pens (15). The strip shows 4 equal parts for the 4 pens, and 3 parts are the 3 pens. Ask: how much does 1 pen cost (5); how much do 3 pens cost (15). Say: find one first, then find many. Answers: $5 and $15.

slides.title: Find one first

blocks.head: STEPS
items: Step 1: find 1. Share the cost equally.
Step 2: find many. Count that many ones.

slides.note: 5 cups cost $15. How much do 2 cups cost? Step 1 finds 1 cup: $15 shared equally among 5 cups. Step 2 finds 2 cups: 2 groups of that. Ask: how much does 1 cup cost (3); how much do 2 cups cost (6). Reveal one step at a time and let children say each number first. Always say find one first.

slides.title: Write the two steps

rows: 2 cups: 2 groups of the cost of 1 cup
head: Step
What we do
Cost in $

blocks.text: Check: 5 cups at $3 each make $15.

slides.note: Write the two steps: Step 1 is 15 shared equally among 5, which is 3. Step 2 is 2 groups of 3, which is 6. Check by putting the cost of one back: 5 groups of $3 is $15. Say each step as a short sentence. Either reading order of a groups line is accepted in a child answer. Answers: $3 and $6.

slides.title: Three words
slides.note: Three words for word problems. Each means for one. A dozen is 12. Such means of the same kind, so 6 such cups are 6 cups the same, with the same price. Ask: what is a dozen (12); a dozen eggs is how many eggs (12); if 3 such cups cost $6, does each cup cost the same (yes). A dozen and such are used in Think harder.

slides.title: A dozen

blocks.text: A dozen cookies is 12 cookies.

slides.note: Count the cookies together: 12. A dozen is 12, whatever it is 12 of. A dozen eggs, a dozen pens. Ask: how many pens are in a dozen (12). This slide is optional to shorten: cut it first if the Mini-lesson runs over.

slides.title: Your turn

blocks.text: How much does 1 pencil cost? How much do 4 pencils cost?

slides.note: Each child works on their own paper with tokens if they like. 6 pencils cost $18. Step 1: 1 pencil costs $3. Step 2: 4 pencils cost 4 groups of $3, which is $12. Walk the cameras; do not ask children to hold papers up. Wait 10 seconds before helping. Answers: $3 and $12.

slides.title: Check: your turn
slides.note: Answers: 1 pencil costs $3 and 4 pencils cost $12. Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Children mark their own in another colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Move and count

blocks.text: Count in twos. Stamp for each one.
Count in fives. Clap for each one.
Stand up. Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Count in twos to 20 and stamp softly on each number, then count in fives to 40 and clap on each number. No equipment, no running, a little clear space. A child may stay seated and tap the table. Do not give prizes or compare children. Then ask everyone to take out the closed check sheet and a pencil, ready for the check.

blocks.head: AISHA SAYS
items: 3 books cost $12.
So 6 books cost $24.

blocks.text: Is Aisha right? How could we check?
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Children test Aisha with tokens: 12 tokens on 3 books is 4 each, and 6 books at 4 each is 24; or 6 books are 2 lots of 3 books, so 2 lots of $12. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: yes. 1 book costs $4, so 6 books cost 6 groups of $4, which is $24. Repeat each child answer in your own words for the recording.

blocks.text: 1 pencil costs $2. 5 apples cost $10.

start.text: 4 pens cost $20. How much does 1 pen cost?
start.hint: Share $20 equally among 4 pens. Use tokens.

start.text: 1 pen costs $3. How much do 4 pens cost? Fill in the blanks.

start.solution: 4 groups of $3 is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, so 4 pens cost $12.

start.text: 6 buns cost $12. How much does 1 bun cost? Look at the strip.
start.hint: The strip has 6 equal parts. Share $12 into 6 parts.
start.solution: $12 shared equally among 6 buns is $2 each. Check: 6 groups of $2 make $12.

start.text: 3 books cost $15. Fill in the blanks. Look at the strip.
start.hint: Find 1 book first. Then find 2 books.
start.solution: $15 shared equally among 3 books is $5 each. 2 books cost 2 groups of $5, which is $10. Check: 3 groups of $5 make $15.

start.text: 4 pens cost $12. Lily says 1 pen costs $4. Look at the picture.

parts.text: Is Lily correct? Circle Yes or No.

start.hint: Put Lily's number back: 4 groups of $4.
start.solution: 4 groups of $4 make $16, not $12. So Lily is not correct. $12 shared equally among 4 pens is $3 each. Check: 4 groups of $3 make $12.

go.text: 2 hats cost $10. 3 scarves cost $18. Jenny buys 1 hat and 2 scarves. Fill in the blanks.
go.solution: $10 shared equally among 2 hats is $5 each. $18 shared equally among 3 scarves is $6 each. 2 scarves cost $12. 1 hat and 2 scarves cost $5 + $12 = $17.

go.text: 6 pens cost $18. Mei has $20. She buys 4 pens. Fill in the blanks.
go.hint: Find 1 pen first, then 4 pens, then what is left from $20.

go.text: Shop A sells 4 pens for $12. Shop B sells 5 pens for $20. Which shop sells 1 pen for less?

parts.text: Circle Shop A or Shop B.

go.hint: Find the cost of 1 pen in each shop first.
go.solution: Shop A: $12 shared among 4 pens is $3. Shop B: $20 shared among 5 pens is $4. $3 is less than $4, so Shop A sells 1 pen for less.

investigation.title: Which pack costs less?
investigation.first: A pack of 2 pens costs $6. How much does 1 pen cost?
investigation.text: A pack of 5 pens costs $15. Does 1 pen cost less in this pack? Why?
investigation.answer: No. In both packs 1 pen costs $3 ($6 shared between 2 pens, and $15 shared among 5 pens), so 1 pen does not cost less in the bigger pack. Finding the price of one lets us compare packs of different sizes.
investigation.look_for: A child who finds $3 for both packs, or who says 1 pen costs the same in both. Credit any clear reason. A child who says the bigger pack costs more is right about the total but has not compared one pen.
mistakes: Saying 1 pen costs less in the pack of 5 because it has more pens.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: if 1 pen costs $3, then 2 pens cost $6 and 3 pens cost $9. Is it always true that more pens cost more? Test it with tokens.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. If 1 pen costs $3, do 2 pens cost $6 and 3 pens cost $9? Test it with tokens.
menu.answer: Yes, when every pen costs the same. Each pen adds another $3: 3, 6, 9. A shop that gives a cheaper price for more pens would break the rule, so we say such pens or each.

menu.title: Make a shop puzzle for your grown-up

menu.rec: Recording: pause. Choose a price for 1 pen. Write the total for some pens. Ask a grown-up to find the price of 1.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check by sharing: with 4 pens at $5 each the total is $20, and $20 shared among 4 pens is $5.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never found the price of one. Use tokens to show how 3 books cost $12, so 1 book costs $4.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Show a grown-up how to share 12 tokens among 3 books to find the cost of 1 book.
menu.answer: 12 tokens shared equally among 3 books is 4 tokens each, so 1 book costs $4.

questions.skill: Groups of the same size and the times sign (Lesson 15), counting in 2s (Lesson 16)
questions.text: Jenny has 3 jars. Each jar has 5 sweets.
questions.say: Question 4. Jenny has 3 jars. Each jar has 5 sweets. Part a: fill in the boxes: blank times blank equals blank. Part b: count in 2s: 2, 4, 6, blank, 10.
questions.solution: 3 groups of 5: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15, so 3 × 5 = 15 (5 × 3 = 15 is also right). Counting in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
questions.right: Both correct (3 and 5 in either order, and 15).
questions.partly: One of the two correct, or the product right with the factors swapped or missing.

questions.skill: Share equally and put into groups (Lesson 17)
questions.text: Siti shares 16 stickers equally among 4 friends. Kumar puts 10 pens into boxes, 2 pens in each box.

parts.text: Each of Siti's friends gets [box] stickers.

questions.say: Question 5. Siti shares 16 stickers equally among 4 friends. Kumar puts 10 pens into boxes, 2 pens in each box. Part a: each of Siti's friends gets blank stickers. Part b: Kumar needs blank boxes.
questions.solution: 16 shared equally among 4 friends is 4 each. 10 pens in groups of 2 make 5 boxes (2, 4, 6, 8, 10).

questions.skill: A times story with a second step (Lesson 18)
questions.text: Mei has 4 bags. Each bag has 5 sweets. She gives 3 sweets to Ben.
questions.say: Question 6. Mei has 4 bags. Each bag has 5 sweets. She gives 3 sweets to Ben. Part a: the bags have blank sweets. Part b: Mei has blank sweets left.
questions.solution: 4 groups of 5 is 20 sweets. She gives 3 away: 20 - 3 = 17.
questions.partly: Part a right and part b wrong (for example 23), or part b right from a wrong part a.

questions.skill: A hidden number in a picture equation, and checking a friend's number (Lesson 19)
questions.text: Each shape is a number. The heart + the heart = 18. Ben says the heart is 8.

parts.text: Is Ben correct? Circle Yes or No. [yesno]

questions.say: Question 7. Each shape is a number. The heart plus the heart equals 18. Ben says the heart is 8. Part a: is Ben correct? Circle Yes or No. Part b: the heart is blank.
questions.solution: 8 + 8 = 16, not 18, so Ben is not correct. 9 + 9 = 18, so the heart is 9.

questions.say: Question 8. 6 buns cost 18 dollars. Part a: 1 bun costs blank dollars. Part b: 4 buns cost blank dollars.
questions.solution: $18 shared equally among 6 buns is $3 each. 4 buns cost 4 groups of $3, which is $12.
questions.partly: Part a right and part b wrong, or part b right from a wrong part a.

optional.skill: Queue counting: 8th from the front and from the back, and checking a claim
optional.text: Think harder (optional). Ravi is 8th from the front and 8th from the back of a line. Mei says there are 16 children in the line.

parts.text: Is Mei correct? Circle Yes or No. [yesno]
There are ___ children in the line.

optional.say: The last question is a Think harder question, and it is optional. You may skip it. Ravi is 8th from the front and 8th from the back of a line. Mei says there are 16 children in the line. Is Mei correct? Circle Yes or No. Then write how many children are in the line.
optional.answer: No; 15 children (7 in front of Ravi, Ravi, and 7 behind him)
optional.solution: There are 7 children in front of Ravi and 7 behind him, and Ravi himself: 7 + 7 + 1 = 15. 8 + 8 = 16 counts Ravi twice.
optional.note: Never scored. Whether the child tried it (right or wrong) adds one neutral line to the note; a skipped item adds nothing.

give: A week before: send the grown-up note (L20_Check_Parent_Note.pdf) and the check sheet (L20_Check_Student.pdf, 3 pages) with the lesson materials. Families print the sheet at 100%, fold it or put it in an envelope, and keep it closed. A family with no printer tells you: arrange another way (for example the make-up slot).
Tell the group in the opening and at s-check1: the check is on your own paper, takes about 20 minutes, is not a race, may be skipped in part, and nothing is shown to the group.

Start at minute 37 and finish by minute 57. Children open the sheet only when you say. The paper lies flat on the table and is never held up. A grown-up sits nearby and may read a question again, but gives no help with answers. Cameras may be on or off.

Read each page aloud, one question at a time (the script has the words). Then leave quiet work time: about 3 minutes for page 1, 3.5 for page 2 and 4 for page 3. Say nothing about right or wrong, and read no answers. A middle child needs about 17 minutes in all; a slower child may finish in the first minutes of the workbook.
Allowed: fingers and counters. Not allowed: a calculator, a grown-up giving answers, looking at the workbook. A child who finishes early turns the sheet over and draws quietly.
After page 2, take a one-minute stretch (stand, shake out, sip water). After page 3, say Pencils down (slide s-check2). Do not collect or look at any sheet.
after: Same day: the grown-up takes ONE clear photo of each of the 3 pages (page flat, taken straight from above, the whole page in view, and the name on each page) and sends them to the program's business WhatsApp, +65 9880 5962, and to no other number. Never to a child, never to a personal phone, never into the class chat.

Within 3 days: the tutor marks from the photos with the key below, opening them only on the program's business WhatsApp (never on a personal phone), and records the result on the tutor record sheet (tutor only). Nothing is written on the child's paper and no mark or score goes back to the child or the group. Accept 5 or 5th for question 1 part a, and either order of 3 and 5 in question 4.

The tutor chooses a progress word for each of the two areas from the bands below and writes the parent note from the templates: the term line, two area lines, one named strength and one next step. Sent only to the parent. No marks, no x out of 8, no ranking, no comparison with other children, no prediction.

Once the note is sent, save the photos to the program's private file store and delete them from the business WhatsApp chat. At the start of next term say to the whole group: thank you for taking the check; there is nothing to share and nothing to fear. Never name a child or an answer.
late: A child who was away or whose family prefers another time: take the check at the make-up slot (a small group, a parent beside the child on camera). The tutor never sits alone with one child on a private call.

A child who joined late: the family may choose to leave out questions for lessons the child did not attend. Mark those questions not taught; they are left out of the strand score, and a strand with no question taught gets no line.
